title: Departing Providence Superintendent to Receive Nearly $200,000
summary: The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez at its Wednesday night meeting. Montañez’s resignation — first announced on Oct. 30 and formally submitted in a Nov. 4 letter — took effect at the end of the day Wednesday. The separation comes about seven […]
content: This article was originally published in Rhode Island Current. The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez at its Wednesday night meeting. Montañez’s resignation — first announced on Oct. 30 and formally submitted in a Nov. 4 letter — took effect at the end of the day Wednesday. The separation comes about seven months before his contract was set to expire. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter The separation agreement was approved in a unanimous 10-0 vote Wednesday night and provides the departing superintendent $152,706.92 in biweekly payments. The payments will begin on Friday and run through July 2, 2027. Montañez will receive an additional $46,968.35 for a little over 54 days of unused vacation time. The unused holiday pay will be disbursed in five installments through mid-January, with the first installment also arriving on Friday. Related This Superintendent Couldn’t Read as a Kid. Now He Wants to Ensure Every Kid Can Montañez will also retain his health insurance through June 30, 2027, and he will be responsible for his share of premiums. The end of Montañez’s superintendency concludes his 30-year career in the Providence school system that began in 1996 when he was a bilingual second-grade teacher at what is now Spaziano Elementary School. Montañez eventually became the school’s assistant principal and then principal, before heading to Leviton Dual Language School to serve as principal for a decade. He became superintendent in 2021, roughly two years into the state takeover of Providence’s public school system. The takeover ended on July 1, after nearly seven years. In farewell remarks at the beginning of Wednesday’s meeting, Montañez urged board members to use their combined power to better the district and students alike. “In order to hit greatness, you have to hit some bumps in the road,” Montañez said. “But you know what’s the difference between sitting there and becoming great is learning from those bumps. “You know you can do great things,” he continued. “You have power. Learn how to use that power to benefit you and benefit our kids.” Montañez spent his own school days in Providence’s classrooms. As a teenager he experienced homelessness and struggled with illiteracy and dyslexia before ultimately dropping out of Hope High School. He went on to obtain his GED and eventually a doctorate in educational leadership from Johnson & Wales University. “I was one of those students that you said, ‘Oh, pobrecito Javier, he can’t do it,’” Montañez said. “Don’t do that. Challenge them, because they will end up surprising you.” The separation agreement notes that Montañez and the board are in harmony on the idea that the district needs a new leader during this time of transition. “The Board and Dr. Montanez now mutually agree that it is in the best interests of the District that the Board have an opportunity to hire a Superintendent of its own choosing to lead the District post state-takeover,” the agreement reads. The separation agreement stipulates that Montañez will stay available to the district in a consulting capacity, specifically to aid incoming interim Superintendent Lendozia Edwards as she adjusts to her new job, which begins Thursday. Montañez’s consulting services will be available through June 30, and the agreement does not require him to report to district offices or work a certain number of hours. Edwards was promoted from her current role as the district’s chief of schools to the interim superintendent position during a Saturday, Nov. 14 meeting of the school board, with the board formally approving her appointment at Wednesday’s meeting. Edwards will serve as the district’s interim leader through June 30, 2028. Her salary is still being negotiated by the School Board. School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said at the meeting that he expects a contract will tentatively be ready by the board’s December meeting. To mark the change in leadership, Montañez ceremonially gifted Edwards with a big key Wednesday night. “I would like to give you the keys to the kingdom,” Montañez said. “And it’s heavy. I usually say the crown is heavy, but that key is heavy.” Outgoing Providence Superintendent Javier Montañez presents incoming Interim Superintendent Lendozia Edwards with a ceremonial key at the Providence School Board meeting Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Screenshot from Providence School Board livestream) Montañez’s contract with Rhode Island Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green was most recently renewed on July 1, 2024, and was set to expire on June 30, 2027. That contract stipulated the terms of his departure from the district, and allowed for the disbursement of Montañez’s remaining salary and benefits if he was terminated without cause, as well as compensation for up to 60 days of vacation time Under the agreement, Montañez cannot receive compensation from the Rhode Island Department of Education through June 30, 2027. The agreement also releases the board from an assortment of potential legal claims by Montañez, which could include alleged violations of state and federal laws governing employment, discrimination, civil rights and open meetings. Excluded from this release is a workers’ compensation case filed in September. It is subject to a separate settlement. As is common in such agreements, a non-disparagement clause prohibits Montañez and board members from making “knowingly false” statements, or statements “made with reckless disregard for the truth,” that could be “reasonably calculated to harm the individual’s reputation.” This provision outlasts the end of Montañez’s payments as well as current board members’ terms in office. “This provision applies from the beginning of the Parties’ relationship into the future, and the Parties agree that they shall never abandon this covenant,” the agreement reads. But Montañez and the School Board had only good things to say about one another at Wednesday night’s meeting. School Board President Stephens acknowledged his relationship with Montañez had not always been rosy. “We haven’t always seen eye to eye, as we know, but the one thing that I’ve never questioned was your integrity, nor have I ever questioned your heart,” Stephens told Montañez. title: Opinion: If AI Does the Junior Work, How Will Young People Become Experienced?
summary: I serve on a local school board and have spent my career in finance and strategy. Those are very different parts of my life, but lately they have led me to the same question: How do people develop judgment and experience if artificial intelligence starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to […]
content: I serve on a local school board and have spent my career in finance and strategy. Those are very different parts of my life, but lately they have led me to the same question: How do people develop judgment and experience if artificial intelligence starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to gain them? Early in my career, I built financial models, checked numbers and prepared presentations. More experienced colleagues reviewed what I’d done, sometimes sending me back to reconsider an assumption that looked perfectly reasonable on paper. With enough practice and feedback, I learned that a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter That work was producing two things at once: an output and a more experienced person. The company received something useful, and I gradually became capable of handling more complicated problems. AI may change the economics of that arrangement. Junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them. If AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply, a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners. The savings are immediate, while developing experienced staff takes years. And even after investing in someone, the employer cannot be certain that person will stay. A company could automate junior assignments now and hire experienced professionals when it needs them. That may be a reasonable decision for one business. But if enough companies make the same choice, where will those experienced workers come from? There are early signs that entry-level hiring is changing. A 2026 study of U.S. software job postings found an almost 15% decline in junior vacancies relative to senior ones following the public arrival of generative AI in late 2022. A U.S. Census Bureau working paper reported weaker initial employment and earnings among graduates of college majors most exposed to AI. These include such jobs as junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates. Neither study proves that AI caused these changes or measures employers’ investments in training. AI may also help beginners learn faster, and some companies may find better ways to train people with it. We cannot assume, however, that every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers. The gap may begin in school AI is also changing how students complete their work. A polished assignment may tell us little about how much a student understands or could reproduce independently. Teachers already work to assess that understanding. As schools decide how AI belongs in education, preserving opportunities for students to practice and demonstrate what they know independently should remain a priority. In a 2025 randomized study of university students, those assigned to study with ChatGPT scored 57.5% on a surprise test 45 days later, compared with 68.5% among students studying without AI. The study was small and measured knowledge retention rather than critical thinking. It does not establish what is happening across K–12 classrooms, and AI used differently may improve learning. Still, I worry about students who become accustomed to relying on AI to complete their assignments and then enter workplaces where the routine tasks that once helped beginners learn have been automated. Employers may expect them to exercise judgment sooner, while offering fewer opportunities to develop it through practice and feedback. Districts already consult employers about changing skill requirements. Those conversations are valuable, although today’s vacancies and lists of required skills can only tell us so much about the work students will encounter several years from now. Conversations with people working in education and workforce development have made me more aware of how difficult that planning can be. Labor-market information often lags behind changes in actual jobs, while educational pathways take years to complete. An occupation may remain in demand even as employers change what they expect from someone applying for the first position. I would like schools and colleges to look further ahead when reviewing career pathways with employers. Alongside the usual discussion of skills and credentials, we should ask how entry-level work is likely to change and where new employees will gain the experience needed to take on greater responsibility. Related Despite Rise of AI, More Skilled Trades Training Needed, Industry Leaders Say There are already internships, apprenticeships and other opportunities to learn through work. Are they giving students meaningful practice and supervision? Will enough opportunities be available as traditional junior roles change? We may also need to reconsider how the costs of developing beginners are shared. Schools on their own cannot replace every disappearing step in a professional career. I worry especially about young people without professional connections. A student whose family knows people in an industry may find introductions, advice or informal opportunities to learn. Someone without those connections depends much more on accessible programs and employers willing to provide a first chance. If those opportunities become scarcer, the differences could grow. Students who already face barriers to entering professional careers may find it even harder to gain the experience employers expect. From my school-board perspective, I would rather see us examine these questions while we still have time to adjust how we prepare students. We may continue to see strong demand for experienced professionals while the opportunities that once helped beginners develop into them become harder to find. The experienced people we need years from now will not simply appear when we need them. Someone has to give them the opportunity to become experienced first.

title: Moms Feared What the Midterms Would Mean for Their Disabled Daughters. Then Came Some Hope.
summary: Yasmina Halim approached this year’s midterms with “a sense of dread.” On election night, the 44-year-old went to bed early after Republicans won the major statewide races in Florida, where she lives with her family. Her 13-year-old daughter, Lily, is dying from a neurodegenerative condition called juvenile Tay-Sachs disease, and Halim works full-time caring for […]
content: This article was originally published in The 19th. Yasmina Halim approached this year’s midterms with “a sense of dread.” On election night, the 44-year-old went to bed early after Republicans won the major statewide races in Florida, where she lives with her family. Her 13-year-old daughter, Lily, is dying from a neurodegenerative condition called juvenile Tay-Sachs disease, and Halim works full-time caring for her. That sense of dread stemmed from looming cuts to Medicaid, as well as attacks on the right to inclusion for people with disabilities like her daughter. But when she woke up on Wednesday morning, things had shifted. Across the nation, Democrats triumphed at the polls, crucially winning majorities in both chambers of Congress. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a front-runner to become speaker in January, said rolling back major cuts to healthcare social safety net programs would be a top priority. For Halim and many family caregivers and disabled people, these Democratic gains and the promise of a legislative agenda that prioritizes trying to undo these cuts are a source of relief. “Until you’re in the thick of it, you really truly don’t realize how much politics is affecting your everyday life.” Yasmina Halim President Donald Trump’s signature legislative policy achievement , the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, raised the cost of buying health insurance for individuals while instituting nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that will take full effect in 2027, driving major reductions over the next decade. Medicaid is the primary funder for the home care services that people rely on to receive assistance in dressing, using the bathroom, eating and more. That funding is statutorily optional, which means when state legislatures need to navigate cuts, they’re often the first on the chopping block. “Until you’re in the thick of it, you really truly don’t realize how much politics is affecting your everyday life,” said Halim, who described the midterm results as giving “us a little hope.” Halim, who describes herself as “purple,” rather than a dyed-in-the-wool Democrat, said her vote is often determined by policies, and specifically disability policy, which became a necessity after her daughter became ill. She hopes that a Democratic majority in Congress will successfully push back against the healthcare cuts and changes that have made her life and her daughter’s life more difficult. She also hopes the top-of-the-ticket losses that Republicans sustained in other states will motivate party leaders in Florida to rethink their priorities. “I hope that the government of Florida realizes just how important it is to protect our special needs children, especially our medically frail and disabled children, and not eliminate our home-based services,” Halim said. She is nervous about the Medicaid work requirements that will kick in January 1 and apply to parents caring for disabled children over the age of 13. There is an exemption for “medical frailty,” but what, precisely, that means is still up in the air after a federal judge struck down the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ proposed definition. Halim will need to prove that she is working, although she isn’t sure how the process will function yet in Florida. She works full-time caring for her daughter through a state program that allows family caregivers to take paid caregiving roles that would otherwise go to home health aides and even skilled nurses. The paid hours she does through the program count toward the requirement. For Halim, the greater administrative requirements will be just one more burden parents of ill and disabled children like her have to face. “Medically frail and special needs parents are already stressed to the max,” Halim said. “We are between appointments, respiratory therapies, nursing, keeping jobs, keeping roofs over our heads.” Across the country, Stephanie Walters, 56, feels a similar mix of hope and anxiety about the near future, post-election. She and her daughter, Shelby, 30, live in Meridian, Idaho. The 19th spoke with them in March about the impact of the proposed dissolution of home care services in their state. Shelby needs significant assistance with her everyday life. The program still exists, but $22 million in cuts did eventually pass. Walters recently struggled to organize Shelby’s redetermination — that is, the process Medicaid recipients must go through every year to demonstrate that they still have a qualifying disability, whether or not that disability is permanent. Shelby has cerebral palsy and intellectual disability, conditions people are born with, and that remain more or less unchanged over the course of a person’s lifetime. Nonetheless, she and Shelby still need to prove, every year, that Shelby is still disabled. “I am hopeful that they can reverse some of the federal impact to Medicaid because they know how important it is.” Stephanie Walters This year, the redetermination was delayed by a few months due to a series of errors. This means that some of Shelby’s care wasn’t funded for a few months. Walters also had to fight for Shelby to receive services she had been approved for and had received in previous years. She couldn’t go to an extension of her day program she’d attended for years. Walters isn’t sure if it was because of cuts or simply bad luck. “There’s a lot of a lot of things that aren’t going the way they’re supposed to be going at Idaho Medicaid,” Walters said. Growing up, Walters’ father was Republican. She voted for Republican candidates for most of her life. But that changed as she got older. “I think the last Republican I voted for was [John] McCain,” Walters said. Her daughter’s disability was not a major force in her shift. Until recently, she felt that those services vital to her care were protected. Instead, she shifted based on her experience as a nurse and her interest in public health. Walters is hopeful about the Democrats’ decisive midterm victories, even if they didn’t reach her home state. She is also excited about the number of healthcare workers who have been elected this session and mentioned licensed physician and former public health advocate Abdul El-Sayed, who won his Senate race in Michigan. “There’s a number of medical professionals who will be part of the new federal change in the House and Senate, and I am hopeful that they can reverse some of the federal impact to Medicaid because they know how important it is,” Walters said. What, realistically, can the House and Senate do for Walters, Halim, and other people with disabilities and family caregivers? “The reality of getting those cuts [reversed], even with the margins, through the Senate and then signed by the same president who proposed those Medicaid cuts, feels like a leap,” said Nicole Jorwic, the chief program officer at Caring Across Generations, which advocates for family caregivers, people with disabilities, older adults and care workers. Rolling back Medicaid cuts and restoring enhanced Affordable Health Care subsidies that expired at the end of 2025 will be a long and complicated process, even with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress starting in January. Any bill would need the president’s signature, which he’s signaled he’s unlikely to provide, or Republican votes to override his veto, which requires two-thirds of both the House and Senate. Unless Democrats use the budget reconciliation process, they would also need 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster. “Frankly, I think that we’re still figuring out the realm of the possible,” Jorwic said. “I don’t think anyone was expecting to see the margins be what they are. Having such a big swing towards Democratic members in both the House and the Senate means that the realm of the possible might be better.”
